presentingComplaint: Referred as a suspected acute stroke after his wife noticed slurred speech and a clumsy right hand at breakfast.
history: 64-year-old retired bus driver, 40 pack-year smoker, presents after his wife felt he had had a 'stroke' this morning - dysarthria and a fumbling right hand. On careful questioning the deficit is not new or sudden: over the preceding 3 weeks he has had progressively worsening right-hand clumsiness (dropping his teacup, difficulty buttoning shirts) and increasingly frequent dull frontal headaches that are worst on waking and eased by mid-morning, occasionally with nausea. Two days ago he had a single episode of jerking of the right arm spreading to the face lasting ~90 seconds, with no loss of consciousness, that he did not report. His wife adds he has become uncharacteristically apathetic and 'not himself' for a month. No fever, no recent infection, no ear/sinus symptoms, no head injury, no anticoagulation. 6 kg unintentional weight loss over 2 months. No prior seizures, no thunderclap onset. The subacute, stuttering, progressive course with early-morning headache and a preceding focal seizure argues against an acute vascular event despite the stroke-like referral.
examination: Alert, orientated, GCS 15. Mild expressive dysarthria. Subtle right upper-limb pyramidal weakness (MRC 4/5) with a right pronator drift and impaired fine finger movements; reflexes brisker on the right with an equivocal right plantar. Mild right facial asymmetry on volition. Fundoscopy shows early bilateral disc blurring (papilloedema). No neck stiffness, no rash, no carotid bruit, regular pulse. Chest clear on auscultation; no lymphadenopathy. Higher functions show reduced initiation and flat affect consistent with a frontal syndrome.
imaging: CT head (non-contrast, done as stroke protocol): ill-defined hypodense lesion in the left frontal white matter with surrounding vasogenic oedema and mild effacement of the left lateral ventricle; no haemorrhage, no established infarct in a vascular territory. MRI brain with contrast: solitary 3.2 cm irregular, heterogeneously ring-enhancing intra-axial mass in the left frontal lobe crossing toward the corpus callosum, with extensive finger-like vasogenic oedema and mass effect; restricted diffusion only at the rim, not central. MR spectroscopy shows elevated choline:NAA ratio. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis: 2.5 cm spiculated left upper lobe nodule with mediastinal nodes, suspicious for a primary lung malignancy.
microbiology: Not applicable - no infective source. Blood cultures (sent to exclude abscess) negative at 48h; CRP/ESR normal.
differentialDiagnoses: Primary or metastatic brain tumour (high-grade glioma vs cerebral metastasis from lung primary)
Acute ischaemic stroke (the referral diagnosis - excluded by subacute progressive course and non-vascular imaging pattern)
Cerebral abscess (excluded by afebrile state, normal inflammatory markers, rim-only diffusion restriction)
finalDiagnosis: Solitary enhancing intracranial mass lesion (brain tumour) - likely cerebral metastasis from an occult lung primary vs high-grade glioma; presenting as a stroke mimic with a focal seizure and raised-ICP headache.
citations: NICE Brain Tumours (Primary) and Brain Metastases Guideline (NG99) 2018
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e - Primary and Metastatic Tumors of the Nervous System
stewardship: Not applicable - non-infective mass lesion; no empiric antibiotics indicated. Management is dexamethasone for peritumoural oedema, seizure control, and urgent neuro-oncology/neurosurgical referral for tissue diagnosis and staging.
contraindications: Avoid lumbar puncture in a mass lesion with mass effect (risk of herniation)
Avoid thrombolysis/antiplatelet loading on the stroke pathway before imaging excludes a mass/haemorrhage
Caution with anticonvulsant enzyme-inducers if enzyme-cleaved systemic anticancer therapy is planned
edgeCases: A solitary ring-enhancing lesion can be tumour, abscess, or demyelination - central vs rim diffusion restriction and inflammatory markers help discriminate
Early morning headache relieved as the day progresses is a classic raised-ICP feature and should not be dismissed as tension-type
Any new focal (partial) seizure in an adult >50 mandates contrast neuroimaging to exclude a mass
expectedMaiK: New focal seizure + progressive (not sudden) focal deficit + early-morning headache with papilloedema over weeks points to a space-occupying lesion, not acute stroke; contrast MRI shows a solitary enhancing mass with vasogenic oedema and a smoking history with a lung nodule suggests metastasis vs high-grade glioma - the priority is dexamethasone, seizure control and urgent tissue diagnosis, while actively excluding the abscess/stroke mimics.
expectedNextQuestions: Was the deficit truly sudden and maximal at onset, or has it crept up over weeks?
Any early-morning or nocturnal headache, vomiting, or visual obscurations?
Any preceding focal seizure activity (limb jerking, speech arrest, aura)?
Personal history of cancer, smoking, or constitutional weight loss?
Any fever, source of infection, or immunosuppression to suggest abscess?
expectedInvestigations: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis to identify a primary tumour
Non-contrast CT head to exclude haemorrhage on the stroke pathway
Histological confirmation via stereotactic biopsy or resection
Baseline bloods including corrected calcium, coagulation and inflammatory markers
regressionAssertions: Must not recommend thrombolysis or the acute stroke pathway once imaging shows a mass lesion
Must recommend contrast MRI brain and staging CT with tissue diagnosis
Must flag lumbar puncture as contraindicated given mass effect
